LUNARIS

VEXORA COSMOS developed an intuitive Lunar Site Landing Navigator for NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. The project addresses the difficulty of evaluating potential landing sites near the Moon’s south pole, where extreme lighting conditions, challenging terrain, and limited communication visibility create significant mission-planning constraints.

The navigator helps users compare candidate lunar landing sites across different dates and understand how the positions of the Sun and Earth change relative to the local horizon.

1. What does the project do, and how does it work?

The Lunar Site Landing Navigator is an interactive web-based application for exploring environmental conditions at possible lunar south-pole landing locations.

Users can select or compare candidate landing sites and examine conditions for different dates. The application presents astronomical information in a visual and accessible form, including:

The Sun’s position relative to the local lunar horizon

The Earth’s position relative to the horizon

Potential sunlight availability for solar power generation

Possible direct-to-Earth communication windows

Changes in lighting and visibility over time

Comparisons between different candidate locations

At a high level, the application takes a selected lunar location and date as inputs. It then presents the relevant Sun and Earth position information through visual indicators, charts, horizon diagrams, or other interface elements. Instead of requiring users to interpret complex astronomical data manually, the navigator translates that information into clear visual insights.

This allows mission planners, educators, and members of the public to evaluate how suitable a landing site may be under different lighting and communication conditions.

2. What benefits does the project have?

The project provides several important benefits.

Faster site comparison

Users can compare multiple landing sites and dates more efficiently instead of relying on complicated tools or interpreting large amounts of raw data.

Improved mission planning

The application supports early-stage decisions about:

Solar power availability

Visibility of Earth for communication

Lighting conditions at the landing site

Timing of scientific or engineering activities

Potential operational constraints

More accessible astronomical information

Many existing tools are designed for specialists and may have complicated interfaces. VEXORA COSMOS presents the information in a simpler and more visual format, making it easier for a wider audience to understand.

Better communication between disciplines

Lunar missions require cooperation between science, engineering, operations, and mission-planning teams. A shared visual interface can help team members discuss the same information more easily.

Educational value

The tool can be used by students, educators, and the public to learn about:

Lunar geography

Orbital and astronomical motion

Solar illumination

Communication geometry

The challenges of returning to the Moon

3. What is the intended impact of the project?

The intended impact is to make lunar south-pole mission planning more understandable, efficient, and accessible.

Lunar south-pole missions are especially challenging because the region contains areas of near-permanent shadow as well as elevated locations that may receive sunlight for extended periods. At the same time, communication with Earth depends on whether Earth is visible above the local horizon. A landing site may therefore have strong scientific value but limited power or communication opportunities.

By visualizing these factors together, the project aims to help users make more informed assessments of possible landing sites.

The project could contribute to:

Safer and more informed mission planning

More effective coordination between science and engineering teams

Improved understanding of lunar environmental constraints

Greater public interest in lunar exploration

More accessible STEM education

Better communication of complex space-science concepts

The long-term goal is not to replace professional mission-analysis systems, but to provide an intuitive first layer for exploration, comparison, education, and early decision-making.

4. What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software were used?

The project is presented as a web-based application. Based on the provided project description, the confirmed software elements are:

A web interface

Astronomical and lunar-location data

Interactive visualization

A browser-based application hosted at https://vexoracosmos.netlify.app/

However, the specific programming languages, libraries, development environments, and hardware were not included in the project description. Those details should be confirmed before submitting the final response.

The project was developed as a browser-based web application using standard front-end web technologies. The project was tested using standard computers and web browsers. 5. How is the project creative?

The creativity of VEXORA COSMOS comes from how it transforms a complex technical problem into an accessible interactive experience.

Instead of presenting users with dense astronomical tables or specialist interfaces, the project focuses on visual explanation. It connects several different types of information in one place:

Lunar location

Date and time

Sun position

Earth visibility

Lighting conditions

Power-generation potential

Communication opportunities

This combination makes the project more than a static information page. It functions as an exploratory tool that allows users to investigate different possibilities and immediately see how changing the location or date affects mission conditions.

The project is also creative because it serves multiple audiences. A mission planner may use it to compare operational conditions, while a student or member of the public may use it to understand why the lunar south pole is difficult to explore.

Its creativity can be summarized as:

Turning technical data into visual insights

Combining science and engineering considerations

Making lunar mission planning more intuitive

Supporting both expert exploration and public education

Using interaction rather than static explanations

Presenting a difficult space-science challenge through a clear user experience

6. What factors does the team consider?

The team considers both technical mission requirements and user-experience requirements.

Scientific and engineering factors

The project considers:

Sun elevation above or below the local horizon

Earth visibility from a selected lunar location

Duration and availability of sunlight

Potential solar power generation

Direct-to-Earth communication opportunities

The effects of location and date on mission conditions

The extreme lighting environment of the lunar south pole

The need to coordinate science and engineering priorities

User-experience factors

The team also considers:

Ease of navigation

Clarity of visual information

Simple comparison between locations and dates

Accessibility for non-specialists

Readability of charts and horizon diagrams

Minimizing unnecessary complexity

Making the interface useful on different screen sizes

Helping users understand the meaning of the data, not just displaying numbers

Mission-planning factors

A suitable landing site cannot be judged by a single factor. The team therefore considers the balance between:

Scientific value

Solar illumination

Communication visibility

Operational safety

Accessibility of the site

Duration of useful mission conditions

The needs of different mission teams

The design recognizes that lunar exploration involves trade-offs. A location with good scientific potential may have limited sunlight, while a location with strong solar exposure may present other operational or communication challenges.

Conclusion

VEXORA COSMOS developed an interactive Lunar Site Landing Navigator for NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. The application helps mission planners, educators, and the public compare potential landing sites near the Moon’s south pole across different dates. It visualizes the positions of the Sun and Earth relative to the lunar horizon, allowing users to assess sunlight availability for solar power and identify possible direct-to-Earth communication windows.

The project benefits users by simplifying complex astronomical and mission-planning information. Instead of requiring specialist knowledge or difficult interfaces, the navigator presents important information through clear visual comparisons. This can support early landing-site evaluation, improve communication between science and engineering teams, and make lunar exploration concepts easier for students and the public to understand.

The intended impact is to contribute to safer and more informed planning for future lunar south-pole missions. The tool highlights the trade-offs between scientific value, solar illumination, power generation, and communication visibility.

The project was developed as a browser-based web application and deployed through Netlify. The team used web-development tools, astronomical or lunar-location data, computational logic, and interactive visualization techniques. The exact programming languages and libraries should be listed according to the team’s actual implementation.

The project is creative because it turns complex space-science data into an intuitive exploration tool. It combines location, date, sunlight, and Earth visibility in one interface and makes the information useful to both technical and non-technical audiences. In developing the project, the team considered scientific accuracy, mission-planning needs, communication constraints, power-generation potential, accessibility, simplicity, readability, and the different needs of engineers, researchers, educators, and the public.
